📌 Governance Snapshots: Why Your Tokens May Not Count in a DAO Vote

Main Points
⏺ Some DAOs calculate voting power using token balances from a specific blockchain block
⏺ Buying tokens after that snapshot may not increase your voting power
⏺ This post explains how balance snapshots work and why purchase timing matters

1️⃣ Core Idea — the protocol records balances at a selected block to determine how many votes each participant receives.
2️⃣ Why It Exists — a fixed reference point prevents voting power from changing every time tokens are transferred during the voting process.
3️⃣ Example — a vote uses balances from block #1000, but you buy tokens at block #1005. Those new tokens won't increase your voting power for that proposal.
4️⃣ Risk Surface — users may buy governance tokens specifically to participate, only to discover the snapshot already happened.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — before buying governance tokens, check the snapshot block, delegation conditions, and voting eligibility rules.

Final Thoughts

DAO governance isn't only about how many tokens you hold. It can also depend on when you held them. Sometimes your voting power is decided before the vote even begins.

Stephen Miller Takes the Wheel: Trump Chooses Confrontation Over Compromise 🚗💥


Trump has sent a powerful signal about the direction of his administration by elevating Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff. 

The decision comes at a politically explosive moment, following major Republican losses in the midterm elections and the prospect of Democrats regaining control of Congress. 

Rather than responding to voters’ dissatisfaction with a course correction, Trump appears ready to double down on the policies and political instincts that have defined his presidency. 

Miller, one of the administration’s most influential hard-liners, is now positioned to become an even more central force in shaping the White House agenda. For Democrats, the appointment is a declaration of political combat. 

Miller has long been associated with the administration’s aggressive immigration strategy, including its mass deportation campaign and tougher enforcement measures. His influence has made him a prime target for congressional critics, who are preparing to use their incoming oversight powers to investigate the administration’s actions.

Robert Garcia, the Democrat expected to lead the House Oversight Committee, has signaled that Miller himself could face intense scrutiny. Immigration enforcement, government spending, detention conditions and the conduct of federal agencies are all likely to become flashpoints in the coming months.

The timing could hardly be more consequential. Trump has recently suggested that cooperation with Democrats might be possible. Miller’s promotion, however, points in a different direction. It places a deeply ideological figure at the center of presidential decision-making just as the administration faces a more hostile Congress.

The change also marks a departure from the management style of outgoing chief of staff Susie Wiles, who was widely viewed as a stabilizing presence inside the White House. Miller brings a far more combative political outlook, raising questions about whether the administration will prioritize negotiation or confrontation.

The consequences may extend beyond Capitol Hill. Business leaders and industry representatives have also expressed concerns about access to the new chief of staff. Companies affected by immigration enforcement could find it increasingly difficult to influence policy or secure meaningful dialogue with the administration.

The immediate challenge for Miller will be balancing Trump’s political ambitions with an increasingly determined opposition. Democrats will have investigative authority, public platforms and the ability to obstruct parts of the president’s legislative agenda. 

The administration, meanwhile, retains executive power and control over federal enforcement priorities.That combination creates the conditions for a prolonged Washington showdown. Budget disputes, immigration policy and congressional investigations could become recurring sources of conflict, increasing the risk of legislative paralysis and another government shutdown.

Miller’s promotion is therefore about more than a personnel change. It offers a glimpse into Trump’s strategy for the final stretch of his presidency: consolidate power, defend the administration’s record and confront political opponents head-on.

Washington may be entering a period in which compromise becomes harder to find — and political warfare becomes the defining feature of the White House.

🌐 Former FBI agent pleads guilty to stealing $2.47M in crypto from 35 investigations 

🔔 Former FBI agent Patrick Steven Yaroch has pleaded guilty to wire fraud and money laundering after stealing approximately $2.47 million in cryptocurrency through nearly 100 unauthorized transfers linked to 35 federal investigations. Yaroch, who previously worked in the bureau’s counterintelligence division, faces a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. U.S. District Judge Patricia Tolliver Giles accepted his guilty plea in Alexandria, Virginia, with sentencing scheduled for March 4, 2027.

📊 Court documents show that Yaroch worked at the FBI’s Boston Division between 2017 and early 2025, where he was assigned to a squad investigating an adversarial nation-state. He subsequently transferred to the Counterintelligence and Espionage Division in February 2025, gaining access to FBI systems containing cryptocurrency credentials obtained during criminal and intelligence investigations. 

⚡️ Prosecutors said his thefts began no later than December 2024, before he moved to the new division. Using credentials associated with investigations outside his authorized activities, Yaroch accessed cryptocurrency wallets and transferred funds without permission. The approximately 100 fraudulent transactions involved credentials connected to 35 separate FBI investigations. Authorities calculated his total illicit proceeds at $2,474,380.66, substantially exceeding the roughly $1 million initially identified when his activities became public.
